b: Infective stage = the cyst (quadrinucleate, 10-15 micrometres), swallowed in faecally contaminated food or water (also sexual and oral-anal contact).
The cyst survives gastric acid; in the small intestine it excysts into eight small trophozoites .
Trophozoites live and multiply in the large intestine lumen (commensal, feeding on bacteria).
As the stool dries they round up into cysts (the diagnostic and transmitting stage in formed stool).
In some patients trophozoites invade the colonic wall , cause ulcers and may enter the portal blood to reach the liver .

b: Eggs in stool are ingested by snail (eggs do not hatch in water).
In snail: miracidium → sporocyst → redia → cercaria.
Cercariae exit snail and penetrate freshwater fish to become metacercaria.
Humans ingest infected fish.
Excyst in duodenum and migrate up bile ducts.

b: Eggs passed in stool hatch in water to release miracidium.
Miracidium infects Lymnaea snail.
Inside snail: sporocyst → redia → cercaria.
Cercariae exit snail and encyst on aquatic vegetation to become metacercaria.
Humans ingest metacercaria on water plants.

Eggs hatch in freshwater, releasing miracidia.

Cercariae emerge from snail and penetrate human skin.

qs.q: During the life cycle of the malaria parasite, where does the sexual stage take place to produce sporozoites?
qs.e: Sexual development takes place in the mosquito gut after ingestion of gametocytes from an infected human, resulting in sporozoites. Asexual replication occurs in human liver cells and red blood cells.

qs.q: In the life cycle of Ascaris lumbricoides, what role do dogs and cats play as intermediate hosts?
o: They play no role as hosts
qs.e: Humans are the only host for Ascaris lumbricoides, meaning there is no intermediate host in its life cycle. Dogs and cats do not harbor this specific human roundworm.
qs.s: Year 3 Medical Parasitology II — CAT: MCQs

qs.q: Which morphological characteristic describes the life cycle of Argasid (soft) ticks regarding host interaction?
o: Feeding on multiple hosts across life stages
Spending entire adult life on a single host
Requiring exactly two hosts to complete cycle
qs.e: Soft ticks (Argasidae) typically feed on multiple hosts across their various life stages. Hard ticks often exhibit distinct host preferences, but Argasids are characterized by multiple rapid blood meals on different hosts.
qs.s: Year 3 Medical Parasitology II — CAT: MCQs

qs.q: During the malaria parasite life cycle inside the human host, sporozoites initially infect which type of cells?
qs.e: When an infected mosquito takes a blood meal, it inoculates sporozoites that infect liver cells and mature into schizonts. Merozoites later go on to invade red blood cells.

qs.q: A 24-year-old student presents with swimmer's itch and hepatosplenic complications after swimming in a freshwater lake in an endemic area. Which unique feature distinguishes the life cycle of this parasite from other trematodes?
o: It lacks a metacercaria stage and infects via direct skin penetration
It requires a secondary intermediate host such as freshwater fish
The eggs must be ingested by the snail before they can hatch
It utilizes aquatic vegetation as the primary site of encystment
qs.e: Schistosoma species are unique because their cercariae directly penetrate human skin without requiring a metacercarial stage. Secondary intermediate hosts are utilized by other flukes like Clonorchis, not Schistosomes.
qs.s: Life Cycles of Medically Important Trematodes (Flukes) — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: During the human asexual phase of the Plasmodium life cycle, what structure is released when liver schizonts rupture after 6 to 15 days?
qs.e: After invading hepatocytes, sporozoites mature into schizonts which rupture and release merozoites into the bloodstream. These merozoites subsequently invade red blood cells to begin the erythrocytic stage.

qs.q: During the sexual phase of the Plasmodium life cycle inside the mosquito vector, what specific fertilized form develops from the fusion of a microgamete and macrogamete before penetrating the gut wall?
qs.e: Fertilization of the male microgamete and female macrogamete forms a zygote, which then matures into an ookinete that penetrates the mosquito gut wall. The ookinete subsequently develops into an oocyst containing sporozoites.

qs.q: Which cestode is noted for having a life cycle that requires only a single host (humans) without needing an intermediate host?
qs.e: Hymenolepis nana is an exception among cestodes because it requires only a single host (humans) to complete its life cycle. Most other tapeworms require two or three hosts.

es.q: Outline the life cycle of a three-host tick.
es.m:
- Eggs hatch into six-legged larvae in the environment.
- Larvae feed on a first host, become engorged, detach and molt into nymphs.
- Nymphs feed on a second host, detach and molt into adults.
- Adults feed and mate on a third host; the engorged female detaches and lays eggs.
- The three hosts need not necessarily be different species; the defining feature is that each active stage feeds on a separate host.

ai.title: Entamoeba histolytica Life Cycle
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Entamoeba histolytica is transmitted via the cyst form in contaminated food or water. In the gut it excysts, multiplies as trophozoites, and may invade tissue or form new cysts for transmission.

sections.p: Entamoeba histolytica is an intestinal protozoan causing amoebic dysentery and extra‑intestinal disease, especially liver abscess, in low‑resource settings.
b: Endemic in East Africa, South Asia and parts of Latin America
Transmission: fecal‑oral ingestion of cysts

sections.p: A unicellular, flagellated protozoan that exists as a dormant cyst (10‑15 µm, quadrinucleate) and an active trophozoite (8‑15 µm, ingests bacteria).
b: Cyst survives gastric acid; trophozoite does not
Trophozoites can lyse colonic epithelium and invade blood vessels

sections.p: Ingestion of cysts leads to excystation in the small intestine, release of eight trophozoites, colonisation of the large intestine, and either stool shedding of cysts or tissue invasion.
b: Cyst → stomach → excystation in duodenum
Trophozoites multiply in colon lumen
Encystation occurs as stool dries, producing transmissible cysts
Invasive disease: trophozoites penetrate mucosa, enter portal circulation, reach liver

t.b: Detects cysts or trophozoites; confirms exposure. If unavailable, use antigen detection kits.
Positive in extra‑intestinal disease; helps differentiate liver abscess from pyogenic abscess.

sections.p: Clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic colonisation to acute dysentery and fulminant liver abscess.
b: Acute dysentery: bloody stools, abdominal cramps, fever
Chronic colitis: weight loss, malnutrition
Liver abscess: right‑upper‑quadrant pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly

sections.p: Combine clinical picture with laboratory confirmation; prioritize tests that are feasible in low‑resource labs.

t.b: Identifies cysts/trophozoites; low sensitivity, but useful when microscopy is the only option.
Higher sensitivity; confirms active infection when microscopy is negative.
Detects hypoechoic liver lesion; guides need for drainage.

sections.p: Eradicate invasive trophozoites and eliminate cyst shedding; reinforce hygiene to break transmission.
b: Metronidazole (or tinidazole) for tissue‑invasive trophozoites – chosen for excellent intracellular activity.
Follow with a luminal agent (paromomycin or iodoquinol) to clear cysts and prevent relapse.
Avoid fluoroquinolones – no activity against protozoa and risk of tendon toxicity in malnourished patients.

sections.p: Focus on the clinical reasoning steps that link exposure, laboratory findings, and management decisions.
b: Key clue: watery‑to‑bloody diarrhea after travel or consumption of untreated water.
Liver abscess in a patient with dysentery points to amoebic cause, not pyogenic.
When microscopy is unavailable, a positive antigen test or serology in a liver lesion is sufficient to start therapy.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration from profuse bloody diarrhea
Signs of septic shock (hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status)
Large, rupturing liver abscess with peritoneal signs

faq.q: Why is a luminal agent needed after metronidazole?
faq.a: Metronidazole kills invasive trophozoites but does not eradicate cysts in the lumen, which can cause relapse.

faq.q: Can a single stool sample confirm infection?
faq.a: No; sensitivity is low. Two samples on separate days increase detection, or use antigen testing.

faq.q: How does HIV infection affect amoebiasis?
faq.a: Immunosuppression increases risk of invasive disease and extra‑intestinal spread.

exam: A 28‑year‑old farmer presents with 5 days of bloody diarrhea and right‑upper‑quadrant pain. What is your next diagnostic step — answer: request stool microscopy or antigen test to confirm E. histolytica because empirical therapy without confirmation may miss bacterial dysentery.

How does the cyst form enable transmission in low‑resource settings — answer: its thick wall resists gastric acid and desiccation, allowing survival in untreated water and on food, making hygiene the main preventive measure.
A patient with a liver lesion and positive serology is started on metronidazole alone. What is missing in management — answer: a luminal agent to eradicate intestinal cysts and prevent recurrence.

Differentiate amoebic liver abscess from pyogenic abscess on ultrasound — answer: amoebic lesions are usually solitary, round, with a thin wall and lack gas; pyogenic often multiloculated with gas bubbles.
Why is metronidazole preferred over chloroquine for invasive disease — answer: chloroquine has no activity against trophozoites; metronidazole penetrates tissue and kills intracellular parasites.
In a setting without antigen kits, what alternative confirms diagnosis — answer: repeat stool microscopy on three consecutive days; if still negative but clinical suspicion high, treat empirically.
What complication can rapidly become fatal in severe amoebic dysentery — answer: toxic megacolon; requires urgent surgical consultation.

Explain why a patient with HIV and low CD4 count is at higher risk of extra‑intestinal amoebiasis — answer: impaired cell‑mediated immunity allows trophozoites to breach the mucosa and enter the portal circulation.
